attribution.note: Marcus's own words. He reprints them from his February essay and reaffirms them in the December post.

semantics.note: The normalised claim keeps the categorical wording: there is no way to encode and guarantee the named broad constraints in Sora or similar generative systems. It is a present-tense observation.

contract.note: The plain reading is broad semantic guarantees for general-purpose generation. That is fair and ordinary. Whether narrow mathematical guarantees count as counterexamples depends on a scope the speaker did not specify, so interpretation decides the result.

evidence.note: Pre-post preprint. It guarantees convex-constraint feasibility in specialised diffusion settings. That is not a guarantee of general physics, truthfulness or object permanence in general-purpose video, so it does not meet the contradiction condition.
The 2 December 2024 version guarantees exact constraint satisfaction for generative PDE systems. This is a restricted mathematical domain, not general-purpose output, so it is context only.

reviews.rationale: The restricted guarantees in e7 and e8 challenge the absolute wording, but they do not cover the general-purpose outputs the contract requires for contradiction. No technical evidence establishes the claimed impossibility, which the support condition requires. The packet settles neither side.

attribution.note: Marcus's own characterisation of the cited Mashable report on Brownlee's review.

semantics.note: 'Looks like' reports what the cited review showed. It is not a probability hedge. The normalised claim keeps the version, the problems and the source qualifier.

contract.note: Reading persistence as failures still occurring, not as no improvement, is a fair and ordinary reading. Treating 'today' as the 9–10 December launch is reasonable.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch post for the deployed December version admits it often generates unrealistic physics. This is a company disclosure, but it cuts against the company's own interest.
Mashable launch-day report, republished on Yahoo. It describes Brownlee finding object-permanence failures and unnatural physics in the December release.

reviews.rationale: The report Marcus cited describes object-permanence and physics failures in the December 2024 Sora release. OpenAI's own launch post concedes unrealistic physics. Both elements of the support condition are met, and no counterevidence appears.

attribution.note: Marcus's own February words, reaffirmed in this post.

semantics.note: 'Won't' is an unqualified forecast with no deadline. The normalised claim matches it.

contract.note: Reading 'solve' as reliable physical consistency, with additional data isolated as the cause, is fair and ordinary. The resolution rules are strict but symmetric for a forecast with no deadline.

evidence.note: Controlled scaling study on research models, not Sora. It suggests scaling alone has limits but is not a decisive result about Sora.
OpenAI's Sora 2 announcement reports better physics but admits it is still imperfect. It does not isolate data as the cause. It is a company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline. The packet contains neither an impossibility result nor a data-only Sora comparison, so the early-resolution rule is not met. Sora 2's improvements are not attributed to data alone. The claim remains unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words. Only the billion-dollar aside is hedged as a guess.

semantics.note: The normalised claim captures repeated failure, with Sora as the latest case. The hedged spending guess is correctly left out.

contract.note: The contract treats this as an observation of repeated failures and flags that 'purely from sense data' can be read two ways. The result depends on that reading and on a reliability threshold the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: November 2024 controlled study. Video models failed to generalise physical laws out of distribution, but they generalised perfectly in distribution. This supports one instance of failure, not repeated failure of the hypothesis in general.
Sora system card. Sora trains with generated captions, so it is not a clean test of learning purely from sense data.

reviews.rationale: One non-Sora study shows out-of-distribution physics failures, but it also shows success within the training distribution. Sora's caption-based training does not clearly match learning 'purely from sense data'. The packet does not show repeated failures of the hypothesis under a settled reading.
